topics.label: 3-Step Search Analysis
topics.text: (1) Was it a government search? (2) Was it reasonable? (3) If unreasonable, should the evidence be excluded?

topics.label: Warrant Requirements
topics.text: Requires particularity (specific place and items), a probable cause affidavit, and following the knock-and-announce rule (unless an exception applies: preventing violence, destruction of evidence, or escape).

topics.label: Five Warrant Exceptions
topics.text: Searches incident to arrest, consent searches, vehicle searches, container searches, and emergency (exigent circumstances) searches.

topics.label: Four Traits of Special-Needs Searches
topics.text: (1) Directed at the general public rather than specific suspects; (2) can still lead to criminal charges; (3) require no warrant or probable cause; (4) judged by balancing government safety/administrative needs against privacy.

topics.label: Other Contexts
topics.text: Airport screenings (advance notice + minimal intrusion), prison searches (Hudson v. Palmer), safety-sensitive public employee drug tests, and public school extracurricular drug testing (Vernonia, Earls).

topics.label: Confession Standards
topics.text: Evaluated under 14th Amendment Due Process (must be voluntary—requiring police coercion), 6th Amendment (right to counsel after formal charges), and 5th Amendment (Miranda protections against compelled self-incrimination).

topics.label: Testimonial vs. Physical Evidence
topics.text: The 5th Amendment protects only testimonial evidence (words/writing), not physical evidence (DNA, blood, fingerprints).

topics.label: When Miranda Applies
topics.text: Requires both Custody + Interrogation. Police deception, emotional appeals, and confronting suspects with evidence do not automatically make a confession involuntary.

topics.label: Three Justifications
topics.text: (1) Protecting constitutional rights, (2) judicial integrity, and (3) deterrence of police misconduct (the primary rationale today).

topics.label: Limits & Exceptions
topics.text: Illegally seized evidence is still allowed in collateral proceedings (grand juries, bail, sentencing), for impeaching a testifying defendant on cross-examination, under inevitable discovery, under the good-faith exception, and when errors are made by non-police (judges/clerks).

dcs.definition: The space within an arrestee’s immediate control where they could reach a weapon or destroy evidence.
Police may automatically conduct a full search of anyone they lawfully take into custodial arrest (does not apply to citations).
Using a valid minor traffic violation to stop a car and investigate an unrelated crime lacking probable cause.
Warrantless searches permitted voluntarily by someone with actual or apparent authority (consent can be withdrawn anytime).
Police with probable cause to believe a car holds contraband may search it without a warrant due to mobility and reduced privacy.
Warrantless, suspicionless searches serving non-criminal administrative or public safety goals.
Cataloging property in police custody to protect owner belongings, prevent false theft claims, and protect officers from danger.
Inventory searches must follow standardized departmental policies rather than acting as a pretext for criminal investigation.
Routine searches at international borders require no warrant or suspicion (strip searches require reasonable suspicion; body-cavity searches require probable cause).
School officials act "in place of a parent" and need only reasonable suspicion to search K–12 students.
Police questioning after a suspect is arrested or deprived of freedom to a degree associated with formal arrest.
The government must prove guilt through independent evidence rather than forcing the accused to confess.
Any phase where substantial rights of the accused are at risk, triggering constitutional counsel protections.
Miranda’s premise that isolated, police-dominated interrogation environments inherently pressure suspects' free will.

dcs.term: "Functional Equivalent of a Question" Test (Rhode Island v. Innis)
dcs.definition: Interrogation includes any police words or actions they should know are reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response.
Secondary evidence derived from an initial unconstitutional search or interrogation is also tainted and inadmissible.
Courts should not validate or participate in unlawful police conduct by admitting tainted evidence.
Excluding tainted evidence removes the incentive for police to violate constitutional rights.
Tainted evidence is admissible if the state proves it would have been found lawfully anyway (Nix v. Williams).
A judge-made rule (like Miranda or the exclusionary rule) designed to prevent constitutional violations before they occur.

cases.name: Chimel v. California
cases.story: Police arrested Chimel inside his home on an arrest warrant and searched his entire three-bedroom house without a search warrant, finding stolen coins.
cases.issue: Can police search an entire home incident to an arrest without a search warrant?
cases.rule: No; searches incident to arrest are limited to the arrestee's person and their "grabbable area".

cases.name: Arizona v. Gant
cases.story: Police arrested Gant for driving with a suspended license, handcuffed him in a patrol car, and then searched his car, finding cocaine.
cases.issue: When can police search a vehicle incident to a recent occupant's arrest?
cases.rule: Only if the arrestee is unsecured and within reaching distance of the cabin, OR it is reasonable to believe evidence of the crime of arrest is inside.

cases.name: Whren v. United States
cases.story: Plainclothes vice officers stopped a truck for failing to signal and speeding, purely hoping to find drugs, and spotted crack cocaine inside.
cases.issue: Is a traffic stop unconstitutional if the officer's real motive is investigating another crime?
cases.rule: No; pretext stops are valid so long as objective probable cause exists for the traffic violation.

cases.name: Illinois v. Rodriguez
cases.story: A woman who had moved out of Rodriguez's apartment used her key to let police inside, where they found drugs; she lacked actual legal authority to consent.
cases.issue: Is a warrantless entry valid if police reasonably, but mistakenly, believe a third party has authority to consent?
cases.rule: Yes, under the apparent authority doctrine (if a reasonable officer would believe the person had common authority).

cases.name: Wyoming v. Houghton
cases.story: During a traffic stop, an officer saw a syringe in the driver's pocket, searched the car, and found drugs inside a passenger's purse on the backseat.
cases.issue: Does probable cause to search a vehicle extend to a passenger's personal belongings?
cases.rule: Yes; officers with probable cause to search a car may search passengers' containers capable of holding the target evidence.

cases.name: State v. Green
cases.story: After arresting Green, officers looked through his parked car's window, saw a razor blade with white residue, unlocked the car, and seized cocaine.
cases.issue: Do police need a warrant or separate exigency to search a parked car after arresting the owner when probable cause exists?
cases.rule: No; under the vehicle exception, probable cause and a readily mobile vehicle are enough for a warrantless search.

cases.name: South Dakota v. Opperman
cases.story: Police impounded Opperman's illegally parked car, followed standard policy to catalog valuables inside, and found marijuana in the unlocked glovebox.
cases.issue: Are routine inventory searches of impounded cars constitutional without a warrant?
cases.rule: Yes, provided they are conducted according to standard, routine procedures rather than investigative pretext.

cases.name: Samson v. California
cases.story: An officer stopped Samson on the street knowing he was on parole—without any suspicion of new crime—searched him, and found methamphetamine.
cases.issue: Can police conduct a suspicionless search of a parolee?
cases.rule: Yes; parolees have severely diminished privacy expectations, making suspicionless searches reasonable.

cases.name: State v. Ellis
cases.story: College RAs entered Ellis’s dorm room during a safety check, spotted drug paraphernalia, and called campus police, who entered without a warrant.
cases.issue: Can police enter a college dorm room without a warrant after RAs discover contraband?
cases.rule: No; college dorm rooms have full Fourth Amendment home protections, so police still need a warrant or valid exception.

cases.name: Maryland v. King
cases.story: After arresting King for felony assault, police took a routine DNA cheek swab during booking, matching him to an unsolved rape case.
cases.issue: Does taking a DNA swab during booking for a serious offense violate the Fourth Amendment?
cases.rule: No; booking DNA swabs for serious arrests are a valid identification procedure like fingerprinting.

cases.name: Miranda v. Arizona
cases.story: Police interrogated Ernesto Miranda in isolation for two hours without informing him of his right to silence or counsel, obtaining a signed confession.
cases.issue: What safeguards are required before custodial interrogation?
cases.rule: Police must give the four Miranda warnings and obtain a knowing, intelligent, and voluntary waiver before custodial questioning.

cases.name: Berkemer v. McCarty
cases.story: An officer pulled McCarty over for weaving, asked roadside questions about drinking (which McCarty admitted), and then arrested him.
cases.issue: Are Miranda warnings required during a routine traffic stop?
cases.rule: No; ordinary traffic stops are brief and public, so they do not constitute Miranda "custody" until formal arrest.

cases.name: Berghuis v. Thompkins
cases.story: After receiving Miranda warnings, Thompkins sat mostly silent for nearly three hours before answering "yes" when asked if he prayed for forgiveness for shooting the victim.
cases.issue: Does staying silent invoke Miranda, and can a suspect waive rights simply by speaking?
cases.rule: Suspects must unambiguously invoke silence to stop questioning; making an uncoerced statement after understanding rights acts as an implied waiver.

cases.name: Colorado v. Connelly
cases.story: Suffering from psychosis, Connelly walked up to a Denver officer and confessed to murder because "the voice of God" told him to.
cases.issue: Is a confession involuntary under Due Process if driven by mental illness without police coercion?
cases.rule: No; coercive police conduct is required for a confession to violate Due Process.

cases.name: State v. S.V.
cases.story: Detectives interrogated a juvenile (S.V.) without notifying his parents beforehand, and continued questioning even after he asked to speak with his parents.
cases.issue: Must police notify parents before questioning a juvenile, and what if the juvenile asks for them?
cases.rule: Prior parental notification is not strictly required, but questioning must stop immediately if a juvenile asks for their parents.

cases.name: Mapp v. Ohio
cases.story: Cleveland police forced their way into Dollree Mapp's home with a fake warrant looking for a bombing suspect and seized obscene books in her basement.
cases.issue: Does the Fourth Amendment exclusionary rule apply to state courts?
cases.rule: Yes; illegally obtained evidence is inadmissible in state criminal trials via the 14th Amendment.

cases.name: Hudson v. Michigan
cases.story: Police had a valid warrant to search Hudson's home for drugs, announced their presence, but waited only 3–5 seconds before entering.
cases.issue: Does violating the "knock-and-announce" rule require excluding evidence found under a valid warrant?
cases.rule: No; knock-and-announce violations do not trigger the exclusionary rule because the social costs outweigh minimal deterrence.

cases.name: Herring v. United States
cases.story: Officers arrested and searched Herring based on a warrant listed in a neighboring county's database that had actually been recalled months earlier, due to a clerk's oversight.
cases.issue: Does the exclusionary rule apply when an illegal arrest stems from isolated police clerical negligence?
cases.rule: No; under the good-faith exception, suppression applies only to deliberate, reckless, or grossly negligent police misconduct (or systemic negligence).

table.name: Chimel v. California
table.takeaway: Search incident to arrest is limited to the "grabbable area".

table.name: Arizona v. Gant
table.takeaway: Vehicle search incident to arrest allowed only if arrestee is unsecured/within reach OR police reasonably believe evidence of the crime of arrest is inside.

table.name: Whren v. U.S.
table.takeaway: Pretext traffic stops are constitutional if objective probable cause exists for a traffic offense.

table.name: Illinois v. Rodriguez
table.takeaway: Warrantless entry is valid if police reasonably rely on a third party's apparent authority to consent.

table.name: Wyoming v. Houghton
table.takeaway: Probable cause to search a car extends to passengers' containers inside.

table.name: State v. Green
table.takeaway: Vehicle exception allows warrantless search of a parked car with probable cause; no extra exigency needed.

table.name: South Dakota v. Opperman
table.takeaway: Inventory searches of impounded cars are valid without a warrant if done via routine procedures.

table.name: Samson v. California
table.takeaway: Suspicionless searches of parolees are constitutional due to severely diminished privacy.

table.name: State v. Ellis
table.takeaway: College dorm rooms have full Fourth Amendment home protection; police need a warrant/exception even if RAs find contraband.

table.name: Maryland v. King
table.takeaway: Routine DNA cheek swabs of arrestees for serious offenses are valid booking procedures.

table.name: Miranda v. Arizona
table.takeaway: Custodial interrogation is inherently coercive; requires 4 warnings and a valid waiver.

table.name: Berkemer v. McCarty
table.takeaway: Routine traffic stops are not "custody" for Miranda purposes.

table.name: Berghuis v. Thompkins
table.takeaway: Suspects must unambiguously invoke silence; speaking after understanding rights is an implied waiver.

table.name: Colorado v. Connelly
table.takeaway: Police coercion is required for an involuntary confession; mental illness alone does not violate Due Process.

table.name: State v. S.V.
table.takeaway: Police need not notify parents before questioning a juvenile, but must stop if the juvenile asks for a parent.

table.name: Mapp v. Ohio
table.takeaway: Incorporated the Exclusionary Rule to all state courts.

table.name: Hudson v. Michigan
table.takeaway: Knock-and-announce violations do not trigger the exclusionary rule.

table.name: Herring v. U.S.
table.takeaway: Isolated police clerical negligence falls under good faith; exclusion requires deliberate, reckless, or grossly negligent conduct.
